Fiber-reinforced reactive nano-epoxy composites show 25% higher strength, 20% higher modulus, and 30% higher toughness compared to pure epoxy.
Fiber-reinforced reactive nano-epoxy composites have improved thermal properties including higher glass transition temperature (Tg) and more stable coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE).
Metal-matrix/hollow-ceramic-sphere composites have a density less than 1.7 g/cm^3, compared to 1.85 g/cm^3 for beryllium.
Metal-matrix/hollow-ceramic-sphere composites can have a modulus as high as 25 Msi (170 GPa), compared to 14 Msi (97 GPa) for aluminum.
Metal-matrix/hollow-ceramic-sphere composites can be processed by conventional machining or electrical-discharge machining.
Piezoelectrically enhanced photocathodes are stable in air and easier to fabricate than cesiated photocathodes, which require fabrication in sealed, evacuated spaces.
Piezoelectrically enhanced photocathodes use the piezoelectric effect to create strong electric fields near the surface, leading to high electron emission.
The iridium-doped ruthenium oxide catalyst is used as a durable and efficient catalyst for the anodic oxidation of water to oxygen in polymer-electrolyte-membrane (PEM) water electrolysis cells.
The iridium doping helps stabilize the ruthenium oxide catalyst at the high oxygen evolution potentials encountered in PEM water electrolysis.
Fiber-reinforced reactive nano-epoxy composites include carbon fibers, glass fibers, aramid fibers, and ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) fibers.
Metal-matrix/hollow-ceramic-sphere composites are relatively inexpensive, lightweight, and stiff, with tailorable thermal and mechanical properties.
Piezoelectrically enhanced photocathodes could be used in microchannel plates, electron-bombarded charge-coupled devices, image tubes, and night-vision goggles.
The iridium-doped ruthenium oxide catalyst was fabricated under flowing argon to allow the iridium to incorporate into the ruthenium oxide.
Piezoelectrically enhanced photocathodes are fabricated by inducing strain in the cathode layers during growth on a substrate to exploit the piezoelectric effect.
